briefing.question: Can you restore the rule of law by means that are themselves irregular? The ends-and-means question, and who judges the judges.
briefing.agreed: Capture or purge, both break the rule of law.
briefing.split: Madison, Hamilton, tenure; Aquinas, means; Machiavelli.

briefing.question: Trust and suspicion in self-government: how far the state may go to guard an election before guarding becomes interfering.
briefing.agreed: Deceit wrongs voters; no verdict before proof.
briefing.split: Hamilton, federal reserve; Madison, states; Beccaria.

briefing.question: Equality versus liberty in a republic: does political freedom mean the right to spend freely, or does it require limits so every citizen's voice counts?
briefing.agreed: Big money can distort; voters should see it.
briefing.split: Madison, liberty; Mill, Rawls, limits; Brandeis, light.

briefing.question: War and peace: when is reaching out to an enemy wisdom, and when is it weakness?
briefing.agreed: Peace is the aim; outreach must be honest.
briefing.split: Augustine, Cicero open; Thucydides, Machiavelli wary.

briefing.question: What is a good man, and who forms him: family, community, the state, or the algorithm?
briefing.agreed: Habit forms men; real grievances need answers.
briefing.split: Plato, city; Burke, Leo XIII, family; Mill, Emerson.

briefing.question: Civility versus liberty: whether a free community is held together by shared restraint or by tolerance of offense.
briefing.agreed: Degrading mockery fails; rules cannot make courtesy.
briefing.split: Mill, liberty; Confucius, Burke, manners; Erasmus.

briefing.question: What does it mean to become an adult, and what do the generations owe each other?
briefing.agreed: Adulthood is character; duties run both ways.
briefing.split: Confucius, reverence; Emerson, self; Smith, wages.

briefing.question: Two cities: how a believer owes loyalty both to the earthly polity and to the Kingdom that judges it.
briefing.agreed: Believers may vote; the Church is no party.
briefing.split: Leo XIII, duty; Rousseau, divided loyalty; Aristotle.

briefing.question: The nature of the person: what makes someone a someone, and can it be built?
briefing.agreed: Machines are not persons; humans stay responsible.
briefing.split: Aquinas, Kant, nature; Locke, Turing, Singer, capacity.

briefing.question: Truth and charity: how to hold a universal truth claim while honoring the conscience of the neighbor who does not share it.
briefing.agreed: Faith is never forced and offered in love.
briefing.split: Pascal, Christ alone; Foucauld, presence; Rahner.

briefing.question: Freedom of conscience: whether faith may ever be compelled, or forbidden, by law.
briefing.agreed: Inward faith cannot be compelled.
briefing.split: Tertullian, Locke, Madison, right; Aquinas, Hobbes, limits.

sittings.headline: Poland's top court seized in a standoff the tribunal calls a coup
sittings.question: Can you restore the rule of law by means that are themselves irregular? The ends-and-means question, and who judges the judges.

setup.text: Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, elected by the governing coalition's Sejm majority, announced she had taken charge of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal and suspended its PiS-era president Bogdan Święczkowski and vice president for a month, as the justice minister moved to strip both of immunity. Riot police secured the building, the tribunal's own account called it a coup d'état, and President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane around mid-flight to return to Warsaw.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Madison speaks first: the report names his Federalist 47 to 51, where he set out, following Montesquieu, why judging must be kept apart from the other powers. Hamilton follows with Federalist 78 on judicial independence and tenure, the clause most at stake when sitting judges are removed. Augustine and Aquinas carry the substantive-justice argument the report calls Augustinian and natural-law: an unjust appointment confers no real authority. Locke wrote on what happens when those in authority exceed the law. Machiavelli is seated because Discourses I.9 is the classic defense of irregular acts that found or restore a republic, and its classic warning. Montesquieu is left off as a separate chair because no verified English text of The Spirit of Laws was fetched tonight; his maxim enters through Madison and Hamilton, who quote it. Juvenal, named for who will guard the guards, is left off because the line comes from a satire on marriage, not on courts. Korwin-Piotrowska, Święczkowski, Tusk, Nawrocki, the justice minister and the European Court of Human Rights are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: can you restore the rule of law by means that are themselves irregular, and who judges the judges? The report gives one side, restoring the rule of law, as saying the previous government packed the tribunal, its leaders have blocked lawfully elected judges and defied a European human-rights ruling, and decisive action is the only way to undo years of lawlessness. The other side, defending the constitution, says that whatever the previous government did, a government using police and prosecutors to remove sitting judges of the top court is the very authoritarian move it claims to be fixing, and some scholars hostile to Święczkowski say the suspension has no legal basis. Scripture puts the old warning sharply: “Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just.” (Romans 3:8) We decide nothing about Polish law tonight. Madison, you begin.

closing.text: Where they agreed: a court captured by a faction and a court purged by a faction are both failures of the rule of law. Where they split: Madison and Hamilton judge any fix by whether it protects judicial independence for the next majority too. Augustine and Aquinas grant that unjust appointments carry no real authority but deny that a good end settles the means. Locke puts the burden on whoever acts outside the law. Machiavelli allows irregular founding acts only if the power is promptly given back.

turn.text: The maxim I defended in the forty-seventh paper is the one both sides in Warsaw claim to serve: “The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.” (Federalist No. 47) Those who seized the tribunal say the previous majority had already gathered the court into its own hands by packing it. Those who resist say the present majority is now gathering it into theirs, with police at the door. Both are describing the same danger, from different years.

turn.text: My answer was never to trust the side that happens to be right this year. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” (Federalist No. 51) A court captured by one party is a broken check; but a court purged by the next party is not a repaired one. The remedy I would look for is one the other departments, and the opposition, can live with when they are next in power: a rule for seating judges that would bind the reformers too.

turn.text: So I am uneasy with both stories. If judges were seated irregularly, their tenure was never rightly theirs, and the reformers have a point. But tenure means nothing if any majority can declare its predecessors' judges illegitimate and send prosecutors after them. Once the sword of the executive is used to settle who sits on the bench, the bench has neither force nor will nor, any longer, judgment.

For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?” (City of God IV.4) A body that carries the name of a court but was arranged to protect one faction is, in my terms, nearer to a band than to a tribunal. That is the instinct the report rightly calls Augustinian on the reformers' side: an unjust appointment confers no real authority.

turn.text: Augustine's point has a precise form in my account of law. A law “it is nothing else than an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated” (Summa Theologica I-II, Q. 90, Art. 4) A measure that fails those marks, made for a party rather than the common good, or by one without authority, is not truly law: “The like are acts of violence rather than laws” (Summa Theologica I-II, Q. 96, Art. 4) The reformers say this describes the old appointments.

turn.text: Yet I added conditions that cut the other way. Even an unjust law may sometimes be obeyed to avoid scandal or disturbance (Summa Theologica I-II, Q. 96, Art. 4, paraphrased). A settled law should be changed only when the gain to the common good outweighs the harm the change itself does (I-II, Q. 97, Art. 2, paraphrased). Even resisting a tyrannical government is wrong when the disturbance harms the people more than the tyranny does (II-II, Q. 42, Art. 2, ad 3, paraphrased). Augustine is right that the end does not settle the means. I would add that prudence asks whether the cure, police in the halls of the high court, brings more disturbance to the common good than the disease it treats.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Locke speaks first because the report names his consent of the governed, and a deceived vote is, on his account, not free consent. Hamilton and Madison wrote the Federalist papers on who regulates federal elections and on the reserved powers of the states, the core of the federalism objection. Blackstone set down that elections must be free from undue influence, which cuts against both a decoy candidate and official pressure. Beccaria is seated for the presumption of innocence the report invokes. Machiavelli wrote on the republic's need for the power to accuse. This table met the same story last night; tonight the question is narrower, about the limit of guarding. Heyman, Peltola, both Sullivans, Trump and the Justice Department are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: trust and suspicion in self-government, and how far the state may go to guard an election before guarding becomes interfering. The report gives one side, protecting the franchise, as saying that if a campaign planted a decoy to confuse voters, that is fraud, and preserving the evidence before Election Day is a modest, prudent step. The other side, federal intrusion, says elections belong to the states, nobody has been charged, the filing does not explain how a ballot could prove confusion, and the president's own statement that he told the department to sue looks like groundwork to contest a loss. No one has been charged, and we decide no facts. Locke, you begin.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Aquinas speaks first because he adopted and defended Boethius's definition of a person, which the report names, and built his account of personhood on it. Turing and Singer, named for the functionalist and capacity-based views, are in copyright and are paraphrased only. Boethius is left off as a separate chair because no verified text of his treatise was fetched tonight; his definition enters through Aquinas. The pope, the Pontifical Academy and the Future of Life Institute are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: the nature of the person. What makes someone a someone, and can it be built?
